plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a cutaway diagram of the Frasch process for mining elemental sulfur from deep underground deposits, depicting three concentric pipes that simultaneously deliver superheated water and compressed air downward and recover liquid sulfur upward. The diagram is divided into three visible strata: an above-ground surface region, a brown soil layer, and a deep yellow solid sulfur deposit at the bottom, where a pool of liquid sulfur collects after the deposit is melted. Labeled arrows trace each fluid pathway: superheated water (170 °C, 10 atm) travels down the outermost pipe (downward arrows) and melts the surrounding sulfur; compressed air, entering from the upper right, travels down the innermost pipe; and the resulting frothy mixture of liquid sulfur, water, and air is forced up through the middle pipe (upward arrows) and exits at the surface to the upper left, labeled "Sulfur, water, and air." The three concentric pipes terminate at the bottom in a curved manifold that directs hot water outward into the deposit and channels the molten sulfur inward toward the rising middle pipe. This figure introduces the Frasch process as a purely physical extraction method that exploits sulfur's low melting point and low density, requiring no underground mining operations and yielding sulfur of 99.5–99.9% purity directly upon surface cooling.

interactionPlan.concept: The Frasch process extracts underground sulfur without mining by using three concentric pipes: superheated water melts the deposit, compressed air lifts the molten sulfur, and the mixture rises to the surface.
elements: three concentric vertical pipes (outer, middle, innermost) extending from above ground into the deposit
above-ground surface region at top
brown soil layer, labeled 'Soil'
yellow solid sulfur deposit layer, labeled 'Solid sulfur deposit'
pool of liquid sulfur at the pipe base, labeled 'Liquid sulfur'
downward arrows in the outer pipe labeled 'Superheated water'
downward arrows in the innermost pipe labeled 'Compressed air' entering upper right
upward arrows in the middle pipe carrying the mixture, exiting upper left labeled 'Sulfur, water, and air'
curved manifold at pipe base directing water outward and molten sulfur inward

interactions.label: Play process flow
interactions.teaches: The three fluid streams run simultaneously and continuously: hot water descends and melts sulfur, air descends and aerates the melt, and the buoyant froth is pushed up the middle pipe — a closed, self-sustaining extraction cycle

interactions.label: Step through phases
interactions.teaches: Each pipe has one distinct job — melting (outer), lifting force (inner air), and product recovery (middle) — and isolating each phase shows why all three are needed together
Hovering each pipe or stratum reveals its role and conditions (e.g. water at ~170 °C under pressure, sulfur's low melting point) without cluttering the diagram

demo_steps.title: Melting the deposit
demo_steps.narration: Superheated water pumped down the outer pipe flows out at the base and melts the surrounding solid sulfur, which collects as a liquid pool.

demo_steps.title: Injecting compressed air
demo_steps.narration: Compressed air descends the innermost pipe and mixes into the molten sulfur, forming a low-density froth.

demo_steps.title: Lifting the sulfur
demo_steps.narration: The air-sulfur-water froth is light enough to be forced up the middle pipe and out at the surface — no miners ever go underground.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Sulfur is extracted entirely from the surface because superheated water exploits its low melting point and compressed air exploits its low density — three concentric pipes turn melting, lifting, and recovery into one continuous physical process.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Vertical cutaway: three nested pipe walls drawn as thick black outlines, with the outer pipe descending into the yellow sulfur deposit at bottom. Above ground the pipes bend into horizontal ports: compressed air in from upper right, superheated water in from mid-right, mixture out upper left. Brown soil band across the middle, yellow deposit below, with a slightly darker liquid-sulfur pool at the pipe base. Flow arrows: downward in the outer and innermost pipes, upward in the middle pipe, curving at the bottom manifold. Animate arrows/particles moving along each path; highlight one phase's path at a time in the stepped mode (e.g. water path in orange-red, air in light blue, mixture in yellow). Labels in plain sans-serif positioned as in the original.

authoredContext:
The Frasch process , illustrated in , is important in the mining of free sulfur from enormous underground deposits in Texas and Louisiana. Superheated water (170 °C and 10 atm pressure) is forced down the outermost of three concentric pipes to the underground deposit. The hot water melts the sulfur. The innermost pipe conducts compressed air into the liquid sulfur. The air forces the liquid sulfur, mixed with air, to flow up through the outlet pipe. Transferring the mixture to large settling vats allows the solid sulfur to separate upon cooling. This sulfur is 99.5% to 99.9% pure and requires no purification for most uses.

The Frasch process is used to mine sulfur from underground deposits.

A diagram is shown in which a vertical tube is embedded on the lower end into a multilayered solid. The upper layer is labeled, “Soil,” and the lower layer is labeled, “Solid sulfur deposit.” A thin tube, beginning at the top of the diagram, leads into the vertical tube to the bottom and is labeled, “Compressed air.” Left-facing and then down-facing arrows are drawn on this inner tube. These arrows then turn upward at the bottom of the tube and are drawn upward to indicate the flow of, “Liquid sulfur,” from the bottom of the diagram to the top outside the inner tube. These arrows lead to a chamber at the top right of the diagram with arrows facing to the left labeled, “Sulfur, water and air.” A horizontal tube in the center right of the diagram leads to the outer tube and arrows drawn downward lead back to the bottom of the diagram. This tube is labeled, “Superheated water.”

Larger amounts of sulfur also come from hydrogen sulfide recovered during the purification of natural gas.

discrepancies: the 'Sulfur, water, and air' outlet arrow is drawn as a single diagonal arrow floating off the port, whereas the source shows a horizontal double-line (pipe-style) exit arrow aligned with the port
all three port arrows (compressed air, superheated water, mixture outlet) are single thin arrows, missing the source's distinctive parallel double-line inlet/outlet styling
a translucent orange phase-highlight glow along the outer pipe and melt pool is visible in the default state — an overlay the source does not have, which slightly alters the figure's clean look
the liquid sulfur pool is rendered as a plain darker rectangular block rather than the organic pooled region at the well base in the source
the source's tapered pipe bottoms and the U-bend where the mixture turns upward are only loosely approximated by simple curved strokes
evaluation.notes: The three-pipe Frasch topology (water down the outer annulus, air down the center, froth up the middle) is correctly built with all key labels and excellent phase-step/animation interactivity, but the diagonal detached outlet arrow, single-line port arrows, and the always-on orange highlight glow make the default state deviate noticeably from the clean source diagram.
action_items: Redraw the 'Sulfur, water, and air' outlet arrow as a horizontal arrow attached to the left port, and give all three ports the source's parallel double-line arrow styling
Start the phase-highlight overlays at zero (or very low) opacity in the default state so the drop-in view matches the source, revealing highlights only when a phase is chosen
Replace the rectangular liquid-sulfur block with a rounded/irregular pool shape hugging the pipe base, and refine the tapered pipe bottoms and U-bend to match the source

feedback.rationale: The concept and topology are correct (concept 5, interactivity 5), but the discrepancies are concrete implementation fixes — arrow styling, default-on highlight glow, pool shape — all executable by the generator without changing the plan.

discrepancies: The liquid sulfur pool at the well base is drawn as a flat dark ochre/brown band (#d9a92f), whereas the source shows a bright glowing yellow-white pool radiating around the pipe tip
The source's pipes have a subtle cream-to-white vertical gradient shading on their interiors; the generated figure uses flat solid fills, losing some of the visual depth of the concentric pipe walls

In the source the compressed-air inlet elbow and the sulfur/water/air outlet port are visibly separated fixtures with the outlet stepped below the top of the outer pipe; in the generated figure the left outlet port geometry is simplified and sits flush with the outer pipe top

The source shows superheated-water arrows continuing down outside the outer pipe and curling outward at the base into the deposit; the generated figure only hints at this with two curved strokes and does not clearly show water exiting into the sulfur layer
evaluation.notes: A faithful and recognizable Frasch-process diagram — three concentric pipes, correct strata colors, correct flow directions, and all source labels present — enhanced by genuinely useful phase highlighting, stepped narration, and a working particle flow animation; main losses are the flat pipe shading, the dark pool color, and the weak depiction of water exiting at the base.
action_items: Recolor the liquid-sulfur pool to a bright yellow/white gradient so it reads as molten sulfur glowing at the pipe base, matching the source
Strengthen the base-of-well flow: draw clear arrows showing superheated water exiting the outer pipe and spreading into the deposit, as the source does
Add a subtle vertical gradient to the pipe interior fills to restore the shaded look of the original pipe walls
Check the 'Liquid sulfur' label contrast against the dark pool band — consider moving it just below the pool or lightening the band
